turn_history.text:
I have: What transformation maps the graph of \(y=f(x) \) to the graph of \( y=f(x-3) \). I got Translation by vector
\(
\left[\begin{array}{l}
0 \\
3
\end{array}\right]
\) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: The correct transformation for \(y=f(x-3)\) is a translation to the right by 3 units, not up. Remember that when subtracting inside the function, it affects the x-values, not the y-values. Make sure to focus on the horizontal shift when working with function transformations.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so it's to the right, not up... but I'm still a bit confused about why subtracting inside the brackets moves it right instead of left? Like, shouldn't minus mean it goes the opposite way?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: When subtracting inside the brackets of a function, it shifts the graph to the right, not left, because it actually affects the x-values in the opposite direction. Think of it like moving the x-axis to the right by the value inside the brackets. Focus on how the input values are affected by the subtraction when determining the direction of the shift.
